iterations.theme: Petra Podobnik on birth, motherhood, empathy and life balance: a conversation with Ana Radišić in the Specijalna bolnica Podobnik

sections.subtitle: What a baby really needs and why mom comes first
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik in a short teaser of the episode explains that a baby in the first year has very few needs
sections.content:
The episode begins with a short teaser in which Petra Podobnik summarizes what she will elaborate on later. According to her words, a baby in the first year of life has very few needs: it needs to be dry, fed and, most importantly, in contact with another person. Podobnik rejects the fear that a child will become „spoiled“ if it is constantly carried in arms.

In addition, she emphasizes that every birth is a personal and unique experience for a woman. Doctors may do it ten or so times in a short period, but for the woman in labor it is often the first or second in her life, so she must be able to remember it the way she would want. She concludes that in the first year, by caring for the mother, the baby is in fact best taken care of as well.

The host Ana Radišić in the teaser poses a question that will run through the entire conversation. If mom is well, then the child is well too, but what is concretely done so that mom is truly well? Podobnik received the question with the words that this is exactly what she wanted to emphasize.

sections.subtitle: The podcast arrives at the Specijalna bolnica Podobnik
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić and Petra Podobnik in the introductory conversation in the hospital premises
sections.content:
Ana Radišić opens the podcast with a poetic introduction about the sea, clouds and a harbor, and then leads the viewers to an unusual location. The episode was recorded in the Specijalna bolnica Podobnik, a place she describes as a space in which a „new world happens“ every day because children there see the light of day „through the hands of wonderful people“.

The guest is Petra Podobnik, about whom Radišić says that she lives and breathes this place, that she loves it exceptionally and that it represents her whole life. Podobnik thanks her for the invitation and announces that the conversation is gladly devoted also to topics that are not exclusively medical.

Radišić adds that the energy of the space is wonderful. The camera crew originally intended to record on one of the hospital terraces with a view of the greenery, but calmer and safer conditions were found inside. The host also notes that Podobnik is this time „in civilian clothes“, although in these premises she is usually seen in a lab coat, and describes her as a very relaxed, simple and exceptionally responsible person.

sections.subtitle: Who Petra is when she takes off the lab coat: mother, partner, friend
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik talks about motherhood as the most important role in life
sections.content:
To the question of who Petra is outside the hospital, Podobnik admits that it is somewhat unusual for her that in this space she is not in a lab coat, because it is the place where she works, where she has patients and babies whom she takes care of daily. But what is outside of work, she emphasizes, is equally important to her.

She puts motherhood in first place. She emphasizes that it is perhaps not the most important to everyone, but that in her life it was a „very transformative experience“. Today it is the role in which she is happiest: she adores being with her two children, and their well-being and health are her priority.

Partnership follows. Podobnik describes it as a healthy, beautiful and supportive relationship which she considers key for the development of every person, and in which she now has the opportunity to enjoy. As most important she also lists friendships, loved ones, and contact and relationships with other people.

Radišić notes that the guest said everything from a personal example. She recalls an interview in which Podobnik said that the moment when a woman brings a new being into the world is complete surrender of control and faith in life, which personally touched the host.

sections.subtitle: Raised in a doctors' family: medicine as a calling
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik talks about her parents who are doctors and growing up with medical topics
sections.content:
Radišić asks whether medicine appeared quite naturally in the life of Petra Podobnik and mentions that her parents are the originators of the idea of the hospital: father from the medical side, mother from the entrepreneurial side, although the mother is also a doctor.

Podobnik explains that she grew up in a house in which both parents are doctors, so medical topics and their way of life were part of everyday life. Her mother is a neurologist, and her father for many years a gynecologist. Before opening their own hospital, eighteen years ago, they worked for a long time in the state system. The daughter even then saw how dedicated they were to the job: they experienced it, and still experience it today, as a calling. The patient was always first for them, they did not complain about the amount of work, and even when they were exhausted, a deep feeling of happiness remained that they do that job.

This is, she says, exactly the reason why they decided on such a big step as running a private institution, which requires great sacrifice and presence, physical presence too, along with organizational and medical obligations.

Podobnik reveals that as a young person she also thought about psychology and even about veterinary medicine, because she loves animals, but her goal was always to work with people. Medicine, she says, naturally imposed itself and at no moment does she regret the choice: it is her calling and she is very happy in the job she does.

- **Mother:** neurologist, worked at Vinogradska
- **Father:** gynecologist, worked at Merkur

To Radišić's question about the wish, as a little girl, to be close to the operating room, Podobnik answers that she often visited her parents on duty shifts. Children of parents who are absent for 24 hours at a time, she interprets, thus get to know the hospital ambience, which is no longer foreign to them, and so they also more often decide themselves on the difficult calling of doctor.

sections.subtitle: The number of births is not important, but presence beside every woman
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik explains why it is important to be present beside every woman in labor
sections.content:
Radišić states that she came to the data about over 6500 babies born in the hands of Petra Podobnik while preparing the conversation. The guest corrects that not everything was literally in her hands, although it could be added up with the specialization. In the maternity ward in eighteen years over seven thousand babies were born, and how many births she herself performed, she no longer counts, because it has long been hundreds and hundreds. She emphasizes that it is a „truly beautiful feeling“.

The message is clear: the number is not important, what is important is to be present beside every woman. Podobnik describes an experience from the time of specialization in the state system, where a large number of patients physically made it impossible to dedicate herself to each as much as she would have liked. Then she thought that for her this birth was perhaps the tenth or twelfth during the duty shift, but for the woman in labor it is the first or second in her life and she must remember it the way she would want.

In overloaded and overbooked systems, she adds, that is impossible to achieve. Therefore the family created a place that „radiates peace“ and in which the number of patients is not so large, so she can dedicate herself to each woman.

To Radišić's remark about a completely individual approach, Podobnik answers affirmatively. She most likes to get to know the patient through several meetings before birth, although that is not possible for everyone. Some live outside Zagreb, so she neither asks for it nor recommends it. Nevertheless, she tries, at least through the last few examinations, to feel how the patient „breathes“: what her expectations, fears and wishes are and how she experiences pregnancy and birth. Only in that way, she explains, can she adapt the approach to her.
keywords: expectations of the woman in labor

sections.subtitle: A doctor with a dose of psychotherapist: empathy as a prerequisite
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik talks about the school of body-oriented psychotherapy and empathy
sections.content:
When Radišić called her a sort of psychologist and psychotherapist, Podobnik responded that formally she is not, but that she tries. She has gone through many schools, among them a five-year school of body-oriented psychotherapy. That education, she says, served more her personal development than the acquiring of „paper“. The methods she learned she applies both on herself and with patients, and their contribution to her approach to life and to her understanding of patients she describes as immeasurable.

Radišić notes that Podobnik has a lot of empathy for women and that her calling in a way requires it. Podobnik agrees: she considers that one cannot be a good doctor in any branch of medicine without at least a certain dose of empathy. She adds that people are born with empathy to a greater or lesser degree, and that she personally has „terribly great empathy“.

Here, however, a second problem arises: setting boundaries. Excessive attachment to others' situations can exhaust one mentally. Over the years, she says, she has learned to set boundaries in a healthy way: to be present and dedicated, but to understand that the other side also has its story, that she is not responsible for everything and that some things simply must happen without her influence.

sections.subtitle: How to step away from a job that never stops
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić asks Petra Podobnik whether it is possible at all to step away from work
sections.content:
Radišić admits that learning to set boundaries is probably very difficult for a person who lives her job, is responsible by nature and works in the most sensitive part of medicine, with children, babies and coming into the world. She recalls that before the recording Podobnik mentioned that several things are happening at the same time: a woman in labor has arrived, and after the birth a cesarean section follows. According to the host, her brain is at every moment „on at least three-four channels“.

Podobnik clarifies that boundaries can refer to different things. In work and in life in general she tries to act from the purest and best intention toward patients and the people around her, although, she says, not every day is the same and sometimes she has no capacity or patience. A boundary can also be that someone who has different ideas does not waste her time.

When it comes to the relationship between doctor and patient, communication is key, according to her words. The doctor should clearly state her experience and what she considers wisest in the given situation, and usually a solution is reached. Patients who have their own vision, and whose plan does not come true, must in some way accept it.

When it comes to work, it is necessary to set healthy boundaries so as not to reach extreme exhaustion. Over the years Podobnik has learned to pass some things on to others, although she still loves to do a lot of things herself. She sees, however, that because of this she runs out of time for things that make her happy. She concludes that life teaches one to set boundaries, and without a feeling of guilt, in a healthy way.

sections.subtitle: Fear, trauma and trust: when a doctor restores the feeling of safety
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik talks about women who have gone through losses and difficult births
sections.content:
Radišić asks with which fears women most often come and what Podobnik is most proud of when she closes the circle, that is, when she discharges the patient from the hospital.

Podobnik answers that, as a distinctly empathetic person with a lot of understanding for people, she feels best with patients who have a greater dose of relaxedness. That is, she admits, hard to achieve. A woman who becomes pregnant may not yet be in a place where she can surrender control and relax completely, and pregnancy and birth are phases of life that are very hard to control. Despite all methods, knowledge, science and ultrasound examinations, some things cannot be predicted or prevented, nor can one intervene medically in everything.

She feels best beside patients who come with trust and are ready to listen to advice. Then the doctors lead them through the entire process and they are surrendered.

She especially loves giving a feeling of safety to women who are in great fear. These are often those who:

- experienced multiple pregnancy losses,
- lost a pregnancy in a later phase, which is an extremely traumatic experience,
- went through very difficult births and have a pronounced fear of birth.

When she devotes attention to such a patient, gives her safety and everything goes well, Podobnik experiences the privilege of being part of that happiness. She calls this the greatest fulfillment a doctor can have. Radišić comments on this that it is beautiful to see and witness how much love the guest invests in the story about her work.

sections.subtitle: Petra as a patient: a birth that cannot be planned
sections.screenshot_description: Ana Radišić asks Petra Podobnik what it was like to be in the role of a patient
sections.content:
Radišić moves to personal experience: what changed in Podobnik as a mother and how it was when, knowing everything about birth, she herself was in the role of patient.

Podobnik admits that she then already knew that nothing can be planned. Her son is now fifteen years old, and her daughter ten, which means that it was quite a few years ago, when she was not yet in the place where she is today. Still, she knew enough that she could deeply surrender control. Everything, she says, happened in the best possible way and extremely quickly, and the son was born first. She remembers that experience as beautiful.

She passes this experience on to her pregnant women as well. Women prepare for birth throughout the whole pregnancy, go through big courses, have a picture in their head of how it should look and set expectations for themselves. Then unfortunately it often happens, says Podobnik, that „the universe“ wants in some way to teach that one needs to surrender control, so the opposite happens.

She tells them that preparation is good, in the form that suits them, and that doctors from the medical side take part in it. But the most important thing is to prepare for what follows, because birth passes in one day. Perhaps its course will not be able to be influenced, but the goal is that it goes best for mother and baby, be it vaginal birth or cesarean section. At the end the feeling of a beautiful, not traumatic experience must remain, that everything happened as it should and that mom and baby are well. „And then motherhood follows“, she concludes.

sections.subtitle: The first year: the baby needs contact, and the mother support, not pressure
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik explains that in the first year a baby needs safety, peace and contact
sections.content:
Radišić returns the conversation to the question from the beginning: how to make mom be well and know what to do. Podobnik describes the baby's needs in the first year as very simple: to be dry, fed and in contact. Other needs, she says, there are none, and in the first year there is not „much psychology“. If a very needy baby is born, one should simply hold it constantly. The claim that a child will „get used to arms“ and become spoiled she considers a myth: people worry too much about concepts that in that phase are not important at all. What matters is that the baby feels safety and peace.

Even more important, according to Podobnik, is that mom is well. A mother is born in a new role, and society imposes a multitude of expectations on her, which can also be seen on social networks. She looks at the solution simply: mom needs to sleep as much as she can, which is difficult in the first months, and when she cannot constantly take care of the baby, others should replace her. It is about a whole „support team“, from the partner, if she has one, to the family.

**What grandmothers and villages used to do**

Podobnik recalls that once „the village raised the child“, which was simpler: someone was always holding the children in their arms and they did not let them cry. She recalls her grandmother, who did not know psychology, and who said that a child must not cry because it will get bread. For her that was deeply unnatural. Later different strategies developed: parents must quickly return to work, and the Western world hurries to teach the child to sleep in its own room. Podobnik considers that unnatural, and for mothers it is hard to reconcile all the expectations of the surroundings.

Therefore the task of the health staff is to provide them in the first days with safety, so that they feel seen and supported, so that someone sits beside them and listens to them when baby blues and the natural drop of hormones catch them and they cry. It should also be shown to them that they can continue to receive such support. Podobnik concludes: care for mom in the first year is absolutely the main care for the baby.

sections.subtitle: Mother, doctor, daughter: the path to the best version of oneself
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik explains how the birth of her son started her work on herself
sections.content:
Radišić thanks her for the answer and asks how Podobnik managed to reconcile all the expectations. She notes that the guest said she had worked a lot on herself, and is at the same time a mother, the successor of a father who set a high bar and earned a great name in gynecology. She also recalls that the hospital was the first in the region, and today is the only such one in Croatia. She asks how to reconcile the expectations of oneself as a mother, gynecologist and daughter.

Podobnik answers that it was „very hard“. The moment that pushed her to begin working on herself was the birth of her son. She wanted to be the best possible version of herself for him, and at that time she still did not have her priorities arranged. She admits that she did not know who she was or what her purpose was and that she was „torn in a hundred directions“ between work, motherhood and many roles in which she struggled to find her way.

The turnaround came spontaneously. While at the beginning she struggled with motherhood and expectations, she learned of Tomislav Kuljiš and the center for natural parenting, as she describes it. There she learned what is „normal and physiological and what every baby needs“. She had no time to read a pile of books, but believed what she heard, because it resonated with her, and began to behave that way.

She realized that with the baby everything is fine and that it is not bad if the baby cries or needs to be in arms constantly. Our reaction and inner defenses and unrest affect how we feel in that situation. Therefore one should start working on oneself: babies came into the world and are entirely fine, and the parent is the one who needs to „work through“ in order to be the best version for the child. Through years of work, with the experience that the job also brings, she came, she says, to a better place for herself. Radišić adds that in that version of herself she can live all the other roles.

sections.subtitle: The greatest reward of the calling: changing someone's experience
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik talks about the greatest happiness at birth and about women with traumas
sections.content:
Radišić speaks about friends, acquaintances and people who experienced the most important role in life right here. She also mentions two men from the team with which she works who, as dads, also had experiences with the Podobnik hospital, and they talked about it unplanned, while the cameras were off. She asks the guest what her personal greatest reward is.

Podobnik says that she is glad to hear such comments, but that they are only a consequence of the feeling that people carry. The greatest happiness she experiences at every birth, when she sees the genuine happiness of the parents at the moment when their baby is born.

Her greatest happiness, however, is when she emotionally connects with someone who has gone through difficult situations, and when she knows that she has perhaps changed their experience so that they will go into life with a different one. That is, she says, personally the most significant in her work. Many of her patients have „terrible traumas“ and physically cannot decide on the next pregnancy, although they want a child. The task of doctors, she explains, is to provide them with safety, because when they go through that moment, that experience will change everything for them.

sections.subtitle: Birth in peace: what the Podobnik hospital offers families
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik describes the peace and privacy after birth in the hospital
sections.content:
Radišić states that she read that in this hospital birth takes place in a „more humane“ way and asks whether that is so. Podobnik confirms that ideally birth could take place like this everywhere. She emphasizes that it is not unattainable in other systems either, but the obstacle is only the number of patients.

She speaks also from the experience of a patient, because she herself gave birth here. She says it is very nice when everyone is dedicated, and the woman in labor has a feeling of peace and does not need to have a hundred people around her, nor hear those who are going through their phases of birth. After birth she stays alone in the room with her baby and they have their moment of bonding, first as a family.

Podobnik calls this a luxury, but in an ideal world it would look like this in every hospital. She adds that in some countries it really does look like this, also in other systems.

sections.subtitle: Love as the essence of everything, and the greatest skill is love for oneself
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik answers what love is for her
sections.content:
Radišić asks Petra Podobnik what love is for her. She says that everyone should strive to become love and to spread it, and the guest, according to her words, does this through work, which is felt at every step of the hospital, and probably in private life too.

Podobnik answers that love is „absolutely the essence of everything“. She admits that this may sound like a generalization, but when one goes deep, it truly is the essence of everything. It includes love for children, partner, friends, loved ones and parents, but also for people in general. She considers that toward every person who comes one should cherish love at some level, with respect and understanding of that person's problem, which for her is also a sign of love.

She considers love for oneself the greatest skill. She emphasizes that she does not mean this from a selfish place, but as a base that is hard to reach. In her opinion it is a lifelong job, and a person can only get a little closer to it through the years, if he devotes himself to it. Whoever is on that base does not act from fear, but from complete trust in life and knows that everything happens for a reason.

Podobnik adds that then a person begins to surround himself with people who radiate in the same way, so good things happen. And the lesser good ones are more easily survived and much is learned from them. Radišić agrees with this.

sections.subtitle: What medicine teaches and the faculty does not: an hour of conversation that calms
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik talks about meeting patients and a conversation that calms
sections.content:
Radišić asks what medicine has taught Petra Podobnik that the faculty has not. Podobnik answers that this refers to everything she spoke about. She has always been, she says, hungry for knowledge and has that trait even today. During her studies, she admits, she studied too much. That created great work habits for her, but from today's perspective she thinks she could have relaxed a little more: she did not have to have all fives, because in the end that is not so important.

The earlier phase of development and specialization she describes as a time when there was a lot of work. She does not regret it and it was not hard for her, because it gave her a base and experience that is now very important to her.

The job itself she describes as wonderful because every day she is in contact with people. She looks forward to the open doors and the fact that she will see there about twenty new couples, perhaps sense that someone has fears or answer their questions. Sometimes patients come to her with a big problem and after an hour of conversation they leave and say: „Now you have calmed us so“, because before that five doctors had given them difficult diagnoses or bad prognoses.

Podobnik emphasizes that doctors cannot influence outcomes, but can influence how a person feels and how much the doctor is beside him in such situations. Radišić comments that this was beautifully said.

sections.subtitle: Gorski kotar, dog, training and the people she loves: how Petra charges her batteries
sections.screenshot_description: Petra Podobnik talks about spending time in nature and free weekends in Gorski kotar
sections.content:
Near the end of the conversation Radišić asks Petra Podobnik how she charges the „batteries of the heart“ and what she likes privately, so that she would be even better on all other fronts, but above all on the personal one.

Podobnik says that over time she realized these are small things, above all being in nature. She is overjoyed when she has a free weekend so she can go to Gorski kotar, from where her grandmother and grandfather are and where they have a house in which she spent the happiest part of her childhood. There, she says, her heart is in place.

These are trifles like a walk through the forest, going out into nature, even in Zagreb if because of work she cannot go far, then quality time with the children and the dog, as well as training. She tries to exercise several times a week, which relaxes her and charges her for what comes next.

The best thing a person can do she considers to be spending time with the people he loves.

**Conclusion and farewell**

Radišić thanks the guest for a wonderful conversation and says that, although the viewers are not gynecologists nor in medicine, they can change a lot in their own lives based on her words. Podobnik, whom the operating room and patients await, says that it is important to be present in the moment in which you are, because then everything somehow falls into place. Radišić adds that at the moment of birth nothing exists outside the operating room, so that same presence should be carried into everyday life: perhaps we are not in a literal operating room, but we are in the „room of our own life“. She invites the viewers to like and comment and announces a new edition of the podcast.
